vignette: He sits on the edge of the examination table, still in his fatigues, the sharp scent of chlorhexidine clinging to his sleeves. At forty-nine, his hands know how to stabilize a cervical spine under desert sun or clamp a bleeding vessel in the back of a Humvee. But they do not know how to steady themselves when the house is quiet. When he finally arrives home, he checks the deadbolt twice. He leaves the porch light on. He tells himself it is just routine, the way it has always been. It begins three years ago, during a visit to his family in the Valley. The monsoon humidity clings to skin and memory. What starts as a disagreement over unpaid debts curdles into something else when his wife's voice rises, then strikes. He has never been a man who breaks easily. He has watched men fracture under fire and tried to keep them whole. But this is different. This is supposed to be his sanctuary. When he wakes on the guest room floor, his jaw throbs and his knuckles are split from trying to block a second blow, he feels a strange detachment, as if he were watching a medic's field report being written about someone else. He cleans himself in silence. He packs his duffel. He drives home without telling anyone. In the months that follow, his body becomes a map of flinches. He still moves through the medic bay with practiced efficiency, barking orders, applying pressure dressings, keeping his voice level. His crew trusts him. But he no longer sleeps through the night. He keeps a heavy flashlight under his pillow. He scans the room the moment he hears the front door open. When his wife asks how his shift went, his throat tightens, and he defaults to clinical jargon, talking about tourniquets and triage tags until the conversation runs out. He pulls away when she reaches for his hand. He tells himself it is fatigue. He tells himself it is duty. He does not tell himself that he is afraid. His training taught him to assess threat instantly: airway, breathing, circulation. Now he applies that same triage to his own life. He notices the tilt of her head, the way her knuckles whiten around a coffee mug, the shift in her tone. He walks on a wire, calculating exits before she finishes her sentences. At work, he catches himself staring at the floor when a colleague raises a voice in frustration. His chest locks. His breath shortens. He steps into the supply closet and counts backward from ten until the room stops spinning. He has stopped attending family gatherings. The weight of what is expected of him-a man who should have handled it, a man who should have been stronger-sits in his ribs like a stone. In his community, there is a quiet script for how men endure hardship. He feels he has broken a page no one else can read, and the shame of that silence has grown heavier than the bruises ever did. Today, he finishes his shift and sits in his truck for twenty minutes before turning the key. The radio plays a steady pulse of static. He thinks about the patient he stabilized this morning, a young soldier who grabbed his arm and whispered thanks. He wants to tell the boy that gratitude is not a tourniquet. He wants to ask for help, but the words catch behind his teeth, sharp and heavy. He drives home anyway. He leaves the porch light on. He unlocks the door and steps inside, ready to pretend he is whole.
